prompt: An emergency room treats the most urgent patient next, no matter who arrived first.
why: The next patient is chosen by urgency, not arrival time. Always taking the most important item next is a priority queue, usually a heap.
trap: Arrival order doesn't decide, so it isn't a queue.

prompt: Keep the top 10 scores as new scores stream in.
tells: top 10 scores as new scores stream in
why: A heap of 10 keeps the smallest of the current top scores on top, so each new score is compared and swapped in quickly. Best-K problems use a heap.
trap: Sorting everything again each time is wasted work.

prompt: A task scheduler always runs the job with the earliest deadline next.
why: The scheduler repeatedly needs the smallest deadline among many jobs. A heap hands you the smallest item quickly every time.

prompt: A maps app repeatedly picks the closest unvisited place to explore next.
why: Each step needs the nearest place not yet visited, out of many choices. Picking the smallest value again and again is what a heap does well.
trap: The map is a graph; choosing the closest uses a heap.

prompt: Merge many sorted lists by always taking the smallest front item.
tells: always taking the smallest front item
why: Put the front of each list in a heap and keep taking the smallest. The heap always knows which front item comes next.

prompt: An airline boards first class before everyone else, then by group number.
why: Order is decided by class and group, not by who got to the gate first. Serving by priority instead of arrival is a priority queue.
